title: What Really Sank the Titanic (It Wasn't Just the Iceberg)
description: The Titanic was called practically unsinkable, and it sank in two hours and forty minutes. The iceberg started it, but the engineering decided it: sixteen watertight compartments with walls that stopped short, a row of narrow openings instead of a giant gash, rivets that researchers say were weaker at the bow, and a split-second turn that may have made things worse. Here's the whole chain, built in low-poly 3D, told with respect for the more than 1,500 people who died.
sources: RMS Titanic (269 m long, 16 watertight compartments, could float with the first four flooded, about 22 knots, collision at 11:40 pm on 14 April 1912, sank at 2:20 am, more than 1,500 died, 20 lifeboats for 1,178 people): Wikipedia, Titanic; Wikipedia, Sinking of the Titanic

Damage: about 90 m along the starboard bow, six narrow openings totalling about 1.1 square metres (1996 sonar survey): Garzke, W. et al., Titanic: The Anatomy of a Disaster, Society of Naval Architects and Marine Engineers Marine Forensics Panel (1997)

Rivets: about three million; steel rivets set by hydraulic machines amidships, wrought-iron rivets hammered by hand at the bow and stern; high slag content in recovered rivets: McCarty, J. H. and Foecke, T., What Really Sank the Titanic (2008); NIST, Metallurgy of steel and rivets from the Titanic
Thomas Andrews' estimate, bulkheads only up to E deck, the 'ice cube tray' flooding: British Wreck Commissioner's Inquiry (1912); US Senate Inquiry (1912)
SS Arizona struck an iceberg head-on in 1879 and reached St. John's: Wikipedia, SS Arizona (1879)
International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (1914) and the International Ice Patrol: International Maritime Organization; US Coast Guard International Ice Patrol
